doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

chapter: Race and the nature of jazz
title: Jelly Roll Morton on jazz origins
summary: Citing Lomax's Mr. Jelly Lord to argue jazz formed in New Orleans from combined influences.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well I mean if you read about the early history of the music from the guys who actually did it, for instance, Alan Lomax’s book about Jelly Roll Morton called Mr. Jelly Lord. Jelly Roll Morton. It’s basically taken from tapes of Jelly Roll Morton talking about the music, and him saying well yeah, we listened to the European musicians and we had such-and-such and Tony Parenti was there, and Tony Parenti was an Italian guy, and so forth. And that’s what it was. It was a combination of the African sounds and rhythms and so forth, but also with European styles and European scales and the music that was developed in Europe. So like I said it’s what made it so unique. I mean if you were going to try to sit there and say this is strictly an African music, it’s not. Because you go to Africa and you listen to what they’re doing, they’re not doing jazz. They’re doing things that jazz had a lot of roots in, but it’s not jazz. Jazz was something that was formed
uniquely there because of the combination of the different ideas and the different musical concepts.
